      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Children</span>'s Health</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Pediatrics</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s health includes physical, mental and social well-being. Most parents know the basics of keeping <span class="qt0">children</span> healthy, like offering them healthy foods, making sure they get enough sleep and exercise and ensuring their safety. </p><p>It is also important for <span class="qt0">children</span> to get regular checkups with their health care provider. These visits are a chance to check your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s development. They are also a good time to catch or prevent problems.</p><p>Other than checkups, <span class="qt0">school-age children</span> should be seen for:</p><ul><li>Significant weight gain or loss</li><li>Sleep problems or change in behavior</li><li>Fever higher than 102</li><li>Rashes or skin infections</li><li>Frequent sore throats</li><li>Breathing problems</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="0" url="https://medlineplus.gov/refluxinchildren.html">
      <content name="title">Reflux in <span class="qt0">Children</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">GERD in <span class="qt0">Children</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Gastroesophageal Reflux in <span class="qt0">Children</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">GER in <span class="qt0">Children</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is reflux (GER) and GERD?<p>Gastroesophageal reflux (GER), often called reflux, occurs when food or stomach acid flows back from your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s stomach into the esophagus. The esophagus is the tube that carries food from your mouth to your stomach. This can sometimes cause irritation or a burning sensation. Occasional reflux is common and usually not a problem.</p><p>Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a more serious and long-lasting type of reflux. GERD can cause repeated symptoms or damage to the lining of the esophagus. Having reflux two or more times a week may be a sign of GERD. Your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s health care provider may diagnose GERD if the reflux causes pain, feeding problems, or irritation of the esophagus.</p>What causes reflux and GERD in <span class="qt0">children</span>?<p>A small muscle called the lower esophageal sphincter acts as a valve between the esophagus and stomach. When your <span class="qt1">child</span> swallows, this muscle relaxes to let food pass from the esophagus to the stomach. This muscle normally stays closed, so the stomach contents and acid don't flow back into the esophagus. This muscle, along with the diaphragm (the large muscle between the chest and abdomen), usually prevents reflux. It's normal for <span class="qt0">children</span> to have reflux occasionally.</p><p>In <span class="qt0">children</span> who have GERD, the lower esophageal sphincter may be weak or relax when it shouldn't. That allows stomach contents into the esophagus. This can happen because of:</p><ul><li>A hiatal hernia, a condition in which the upper part of the stomach pushes up into the chest</li><li>Increased pressure on the abdomen (belly) from being overweight or having obesity</li><li>Certain medicines, such as some used to treat asthma, allergies, depression, or pain</li><li>Smoking or exposure to secondhand smoke</li><li>Previous surgery on the esophagus or upper abdomen</li><li>Developmental delays or certain neurological conditions, such as cerebral palsy</li><li>Lung conditions, such as cystic fibrosis</li></ul>How common are reflux and GERD in <span class="qt0">children</span>?<p>Many <span class="qt0">children</span> have occasional reflux, especially after large meals or physical activity. GERD is less common, and most symptoms improve with time and lifestyle changes. </p>What are the symptoms of reflux and GERD in <span class="qt0">children</span>?<p>Symptoms may vary by age. Some <span class="qt0">children</span> might not even notice reflux, while others may taste food or stomach acid in the back of their mouth.</p><p>In <span class="qt0">children</span>, GERD can cause:</p><ul><li>Heartburn, a burning feeling in the chest or throat (more common in older <span class="qt0">children and teens</span>)</li><li>Bad breath</li><li>Nausea or vomiting</li><li>Trouble or pain when swallowing</li><li>Cough, hoarseness, or breathing problems</li><li>Wearing away of tooth enamel from stomach acid</li></ul><p>Other conditions can cause similar symptoms. Talk to your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s provider if symptoms happen often or make eating, sleeping, or daily activities difficult.</p>How are reflux and GERD diagnosed in <span class="qt0">children</span>?<p>In most cases, your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s provider can tell if it's reflux by learning about your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s symptoms and health history. Tests are usually needed only if symptoms don't get better with lifestyle changes or medicines, or if another health problem is suspected.</p><p>Common tests include:</p><ul><li>Upper GI series, which looks at the shape of your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s upper GI (gastrointestinal) tract. Your <span class="qt1">child</span> will drink or eat a chalky-tasting liquid called barium. For young <span class="qt0">children</span>, the barium is mixed in with a bottle or other food. Several x-rays are taken to track the barium as it goes through your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s esophagus and stomach.</li><li>Esophageal pH and impedance monitoring, which measures the amount of acid or liquid in your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s esophagus. A thin flexible tube is placed through their nose into the stomach. The end of the tube in the esophagus measures when and how much acid comes up into the esophagus. The other end of the tube attaches to a monitor that records the measurements. Your <span class="qt1">child</span> will wear the tube for 24 hours. They may need to stay in the hospital during the test.</li><li>Upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy and biopsy, which uses an endoscope, a long, flexible tube with a light and camera at the end of it. An endoscope is inserted down your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine. While looking at the pictures from the endoscope, tissue samples (biopsy) may be taken.</li></ul>What lifestyle changes can help treat my <span class="qt1">child</span>'s reflux or GERD?<p>Simple lifestyle changes can often improve symptoms. Examples include:</p><ul><li>Maintaining a healthy weight.</li><li>Eating smaller meals.</li><li>Avoiding high-fat foods or other trigger foods that cause symptoms.</li><li>Wearing loose-fitting clothing around the abdomen (belly).</li><li>Staying upright for 3 hours after meals and avoiding slouching when sitting.</li><li>Sleeping with the head of the bed raised 6 to 8 inches.</li></ul>What are the treatments for my <span class="qt1">child</span>'s GERD?<p>If lifestyle changes aren't enough, your provider may recommend medicine to reduce stomach acid. The medicines work by lowering the amount of acid your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s stomach makes. Some are available over-the-counter, while others need a prescription. Do not give your <span class="qt1">child</span> any medicine unless your provider recommends it.</p><p>If symptoms don't get better or are severe, your provider may refer you to a doctor who treats stomach and digestion problems in <span class="qt0">children</span>. In rare cases, surgery may be considered.</p><p>If GERD isn't treated, it can cause problems such as inflammation or scarring in the esophagus, changes in its lining (Barrett's esophagus), or make breathing problems, like asthma, worse.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/childdentalhealth.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Child</span> Dental Health</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dental Health, <span class="qt1">Child</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dental Sealants</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Oral Health, <span class="qt1">Child</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Healthy teeth are important to your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s overall health. From the time your <span class="qt1">child</span> is born, there are things you can do to promote healthy teeth and prevent cavities. For babies, you should clean teeth with a soft, clean cloth or baby's toothbrush.  Avoid putting the baby to bed with a bottle and check teeth regularly for spots or stains.</p><p>For all <span class="qt0">children</span>, you should:</p><ul><li>Start using a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste when they are two years old. You might start sooner, if a dentist or doctor suggests it.</li><li>Provide healthy foods and limit sweet snacks and drinks</li><li>Schedule regular dental check-ups </li></ul><p>Forming good habits at a young age can help your <span class="qt1">child</span> have healthy teeth for life. </p><p>NIH: National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/childsexualabuse.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Child</span> Sexual Abuse</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1">Child</span> Molestation</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sexual Abuse of <span class="qt0">Children</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Sexual abuse is one form of <span class="qt1">child</span> abuse. It includes a wide range of actions between a <span class="qt1">child</span> and an adult or older <span class="qt1">child</span>. Often these involve body contact, but not always. Exposing one's genitals to <span class="qt0">children</span> or pressuring them for sex is sexual abuse. Using a <span class="qt1">child</span> for pornography is also sexual abuse.</p><p>Most sexual abusers know the <span class="qt1">child</span> they abuse. They may be family friends, neighbors or babysitters. About one-third of abusers are related to the <span class="qt1">child</span>. Most abusers are men. If you think a <span class="qt1">child</span> may have been abused, it's important to report it.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/childmentalhealth.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Child</span> Mental Health</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mental Health, <span class="qt1">Child</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>It's important to recognize and treat mental illnesses in <span class="qt0">children</span> early on.  Once mental illness develops, it becomes a regular part of your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s behavior. This makes it more difficult to treat.</p><p>But it's not always easy to know when your <span class="qt1">child</span> has a serious problem. Everyday stresses can cause changes in your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s behavior. For example, getting a new brother or sister or going to a new school may cause a <span class="qt1">child</span> to temporarily act out. Warning signs that it might be a more serious problem include:</p><ul><li>Problems in more than one setting (at school, at home, with peers)</li><li>Changes in appetite or sleep</li><li>Social withdrawal or fear of things he or she did not used to be not afraid of</li><li>Returning to behaviors more common in younger <span class="qt0">children</span>, such as bedwetting</li><li>Signs of being upset, such as sadness or tearfulness</li><li>Signs of self-destructive behavior, such as head-banging or suddenly getting hurt often</li><li>Repeated thoughts of death</li></ul><p>To diagnose mental health problems, the doctor or mental health specialist looks at your <span class="qt1">child</span>'s signs and symptoms, medical history, and family history. Treatments include medicines and talk therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>
